source.text:
There's a lot going on here. As for the corruption of the administration, I'm sorry but this is just a drop in the ocean. This administration used the military to kidnap a foreign head of state and steal that country's oil. It's still unclear where the money went for selling Venezuelan oil. Trump himself has made billions since returning to office. The war in Iran has been manipulated for great profit. That's literally killing people to make money. And it's doing way more damage to American Empire (if you believe in that sort of thing) than the chips scandal is.

The big issue is what to do with China and AI and this has two broad restrictions:

1. The US restricts a Dutch company (ASML) from exporting EUV lithography machines to China so it can't build leading-edge chips. Interestingly, the bulk of them get sent to Taiwan instead, which is obviously a politically contentious region; and

2. Export restrictions prevent the sale of GPUs to China.

One thing I'll agree on with Jensen Huang was that (2) was a mistake. China's demand for AI chips is temporary. By 2030 or so they'll be making their own. There is no way for the West to maintain a monopoly on chips so, as Jensen argues, you may as well make money selling them chips in the interim.

But here's the big problem: by not selling GPUs (unrestricted), the US has inadvertently created captive Chinese domestic demand for Chinese made chips because they can't buy them otherwise. That's going to kickstart the domestic industry. If you instead flooded the Chinese market with Western chips then Chinese chips would have to compete with Western chips.

That train has sailed. It's too late to turn it around now.

As an aside, export restrictions have limited success. You've just created a profit opportunity for somebody to smuggle those goods. We find American-made chips in Russian munitions despite 4+ years of broad sanctions.

But the real battle here is over the models. The US wants to "own" or "win" AI with a massive moat on the software. I believe this battle is already lost. Frontier models are thought to have only a 6-12 month lead over Chinese open weight models.

China has decided it is in its national interest not to be beholden to Western software, platforms or hardware. It's why so many Western companies have limited or no access to the Chinese market. I believe this was the correct decision for China. Also, China believes that AI and automation should benefit and be owned by society and not just mint a few trillionaires.

China is just doing the Microsoft model of the 1990s where Microsoft killed Netscape by bundling and giving away a browser. Google then killed Microsoft's stranglehold by giving away a browser. China is giving away AI models and this is a huge future risk to SpaceX, OpenAI and Anthropic and (IMHO) means the US has already lost that strategic fight.

The author mentions that other countries are acting like the US is an empire in decgline. Yes, they are. Because they're correct.
